items.title: Undoing Brexit is the right thing to attempt – but sadly, I can't see Andy Burnham pulling it off | Paul Taylor
items.summary:
Brussels rolled out a warm welcome for the PM but toxic UK politics around rejoining have not gone away

Despite the beaming smiles and the symbolic triple handshake, the summit intended to reset the UK’s tortured relationship with the EU showed just how difficult undoing Brexit will be a decade after Britons voted to leave.

To be sure, Brussels laid on a warm welcome. Andy Burnham’s first summit with the heads of the EU institutions felt like the homecoming of an old friend who had been away too long, rather than a meeting to settle some awkward leftovers of a bitter divorce.

Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

The party's projected majority will surpass its post-election totals in every election since Bill Clinton first won the presidency in 1992, when Democrats secured 258 seats, the outlet said. The party's next-largest showing reportedly came in 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president and Democrats…

items.title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial
items.summary:
The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. items.title: Newsom's bid to empty California's death row collides with voters' repeated rejection of abolition
items.summary:
A lawsuit challenging Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute 548 death sentences is raising questions about the governor's clemency powers, with a legal expert arguing Newsom is using his gubernatorial authority to circumvent the will of voters who have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish capital punishment.

Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he intends to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the Golden State's death row to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, a move that will take effect only after the necessary legal steps are completed.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF) on Sunday filed a lawsuit at the California Supreme Court seeking to block Newsom's proposed sweeping commutation, citing the governor's "failure to provide legally required notice to district attorneys and his disregard for the rights of victims and their families to be notified and heard," according to a news release.

Newsom may be using clemency to impose his own views on capital punishment despite voters repeatedly rejecting abolition, Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow for Courts and the Constitution at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.
items.t: Newsom's bid to empty California's death row collides with voters' repeated rejection of abolition

items.title: $275M Obama-era solar fraud case could net taxpayers $1B, but Trump's DOJ backs Biden dismissal
items.summary:
This article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating the Crescent Dunes solar power plant in Nevada. You can read Part 1 here.

The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing.

Yet investors in a failed Obama-era solar plant are questioning why President Donald Trump's own Justice Department is fighting to squash their fraud lawsuit over a $275 million federal grant — a case they say could recover up to $1 billion for taxpayers.

The investors allege that Spanish construction giant ACS and companies to tied its former subsidiary Cobra, misled federal officials into approving the grant by claiming the troubled solar plant was ready for use, even though it had suffered major construction problems and was shut down for months following a molten-salt-tank failure.

The lawsuit centers on the beleaguered Crescent Dunes solar plant, a billion-dollar, government-backed project that began operating in Nevada in 2015 but was later plagued by engineering failures, repeated shutdowns and two bankruptcies before being sold for just $7 million in July.
items.t: $275M Obama-era solar fraud case could net taxpayers $1B, but Trump's DOJ backs Biden dismissal

Forget the smell. You could almost taste the madeleines. Those late nights in Brussels from 10 years ago when time had lost all meaning. So it seemed it might be on Friday. A press conference scheduled for 12.30pm pushed back a quarter of an hour. And then another 15 minutes. Yet another 15 minutes. There are few things the EU does better than taking negotiations down to the wire.

António Costa, president of the European Council, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Andy Burnham presented themselves as the perfect throuple. It had been love at first sight, and they couldn’t wait for their next tryst. They could barely take their eyes off one another. items.title: Trump inspired a blue revolution. Can Democrats meet the moment? | Dana R Fisher
items.summary:
Political participation – in meetings, boycotts and demonstrations – has increased since Trump took office. It’s time for change

Over the past two years, Americans have watched as the Trump administration enacted Project 2025 and the US has descended into a state of lawless authoritarianism. Instead of sinking into a state of paralysis, though, Americans rose up to push back against the attacks, including limitations of voting rights and manipulations of political power through the gerrymandering of congressional districts.

Donald Trump’s actions motivated resistance in the streets in the form of large-scale public demonstrations, along with more localized mobilizations against ICE and the occupation of American cities. On 3 November, the collective response manifested as resistance at the ballot box.

Continue reading...
items.t: Trump inspired a blue revolution. Can Democrats meet the moment? | Dana R Fisher

items.title: Could Pete Buttigieg win the White House in 2028? | Politics Weekly America
items.summary:
Democrats who might be thinking of launching a presidential run in 2028 are starting to make moves. One such contender is Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary under Joe Biden. Is he the candidate who can unite the broad church in his party?

There’s also talk that a vote to elect the new Senate leader could be moved up, helping Chuck Schumer retain power, after Chris Van Hollen challenged him for the position.

Jonathan Freedland speaks to Marianna Sotomayor of Puck News about the Democrats looking to shore up power on Capitol Hill and potentially head for the White House

items.title: Measles is officially back in the USA. Will Maha pay the price? - video
items.summary:
This week the US lost its measles elimination status, an official recognition that the infectious disease is endemic in the country after being eliminated for 26 years. To find out what this means in practical terms for citizens, Ian Sample hears from the Guardian US health reporter Jessica Glenza. She explains why it comes at an already difficult time for the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, and his Make America Healthy Again movement, and what newly elected Democrats will be focusing on when it comes to health

items.title: ‘You’ve got me for life’: first ceremonies in England cement care leavers’ relationships
items.summary:
Lifelong guardianship ceremonies were announced in July as way to publicly affirm chosen connections

Allan was 14 years old and had been through eight foster families and a stint in a children’s home when he began living with foster carer Russ in Kettering – a move that would change the course of his life.

Russ, 63, fought for Allan to get the school placements he needed and took him to kickboxing every week, eventually joining in himself. When Allan turned 18, he moved out into his own flat, but the pair have stayed close.

items.title: After a blue wave, Trump will dig in his heels. We must be more vigilant than ever | Steve Cohen and Michael Shank
items.summary:
Anti-democratic behaviors won’t disappear overnight. The new Congress – and all of us – must rise to the occasion

Americans just witnessed a blue tsunami in the midterm elections, with historic firsts across many US states: the country’s first female Black governor, first female Native American governor, first Muslim US senator, and more.

And while the voters’ repudiation of Donald Trump’s agenda is clear, as Democrats seize the majority of both chambers of Congress, the work to defend our institutions from further democratic backsliding won’t ease up overnight.

He is responsible for the health of the American people. On his watch, thousands have become seriously ill

At least 11 Americans have died of measles since January 2025 – the month before Robert F Kennedy Jr became secretary of Health and Human Services.

One of Friday’s victims was a child, in Wisconsin, where a baby died of measles the week before. Pennsylvania has not disclosed the age of the other person.
